passage:
"Chinmay, dinner."
"Not hungry."
"You barely ate lunch." Thomas sat on the bed beside his son. "Are you thinking about Ajoba?"
"When is he coming back?"
"He isn't, Chinmay. His body stopped working. We talked about this."
"But who will take me to the temple fair?"
Thomas breathed. "I don't know yet. I miss him too."
Chinmay stared at the wall, then jumped up. "Can I play with my cars?"
"Of course."
Half an hour later he was back at the door, small. "Papa, was he scared?" Thomas held him. "I don't think so. He was sleepy and comfortable."

qa.q: What did Chinmay ask about the temple fair?
qa.a: He asked, "But who will take me to the temple fair?"

qa.q: What did Chinmay's repeated questions and sudden play suggest he was feeling about Ajoba, and what else could they mean?
qa.a: They suggest he was sad and trying to understand what death means, and needed a break through play. It might also be that he was scared or confused, as his question about Ajoba being scared shows.

qa.q: What can Thomas keep doing to help Chinmay through this?
qa.a: He can keep answering honestly and simply, keep dinner and bedtime steady, and let Chinmay play and return to his questions.

qa.q: How might Thomas be feeling as he answers Chinmay?
qa.a: Thomas says he misses Ajoba too, so he is also grieving. He answers gently even though it is hard.

grounding: A child grieving a grandparent asks repeated questions, plays, then withdraws, and honest answers and routine protect him.

passage: I'm Gurpreet, and when my grandfather died I was ten. I cried at the funeral, then ate two jalebis at the gathering and felt bad for it. At school the next day I played cricket as if nothing had happened. Then in maths I suddenly went silent and put my head on the desk. Nirmala, my class teacher, didn't tell me to sit up. She put a glass of water beside me and said, "Take your time." At home Mummy asked me each night what I missed most. I said "his stories" for many days. I kept asking her, "Is he really never coming back?" Each time she said, "No. He died, but we can remember him." That helped me keep going, even when I felt strange about being okay.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet eat at the gathering?
qa.a: Gurpreet ate two jalebis at the gathering.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt when playing cricket and then going silent in maths, and why did the jalebis feel wrong?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably felt grief that came in bursts, sometimes hidden by play. The jalebis felt wrong because enjoying anything seemed strange while Gurpreet was sad.

qa.q: How could adults help a child who grieves in bursts?
qa.a: They can keep routines steady, answer repeated questions honestly, as Mummy did, let the child rest or play, and ask gently what the child misses.

qa.q: How does Nirmala's response affect Gurpreet?
qa.a: Nirmala gives Gurpreet space and water without asking Gurpreet to sit up, so Gurpreet feels allowed to be sad in class.

grounding: A child grieving a grandparent cries, plays normally, then suddenly withdraws; steady routines and honest answers protect the child.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Monday
Farhan's Dadi died last week. Today he cried in Hindi class when the teacher read a story about a grandmother. He asked me three times, "Will Dadi's bed stay in our house?" I told him each time, gently, that his family would decide, and that Dadi had died and would not come back.
At break he played cricket and shouted and laughed with his friends as usual. After break he sat alone on the steps and didn't want to go back to class.
I stayed with him and kept his routine as normal as I could: same lunch, same seat. I phoned his mother after school so we could share what we are both seeing and plan the week together.
- Ms Anjali, school counsellor

qa.q: What did Farhan ask the counsellor three times?
qa.a: "Will Dadi's bed stay in our house?"

qa.q: What might Farhan's switch from laughing at cricket to sitting alone show about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It shows grief coming in bursts: he could enjoy play for a while, then feel sad and heavy again and want to be alone.

qa.q: What steps did Ms Anjali take that protect Farhan?
qa.a: She answered his questions honestly each time, kept his routine steady, stayed with him, and spoke to his mother the same day.

qa.q: How might Farhan's classmates see his sudden change after break?
qa.a: They might be confused, since he was laughing at cricket, not knowing that grief can come and go like this.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a grieving child crying, asking repeated questions, playing, and withdrawing, and the adult keeping routine and giving honest answers.

passage:
Thursday
Nani died on Sunday. Today I played ludo with my cousin Mehak and we laughed so much about her cheating. Then I saw Nani's glasses on the shelf and I stopped laughing. I felt bad for laughing at all.
I asked Mummy again tonight, "Is Nani really never coming back?" I know the answer. I just keep asking.
Mummy said, "No, beta, Nani won't come back. It's okay to laugh. Nani loved your laughing." She said we will still have Sunday pakoras like Nani made.
I cried a lot, and then I felt a little better.
- Devika

qa.q: What did Devika see on the shelf that made the laughing stop?
qa.a: Nani's glasses.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling after laughing with Mehak?
qa.a: Devika felt guilty for laughing, and sad when seeing Nani's glasses.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped?
qa.a: She gave an honest answer again, said laughing was okay, and kept a familiar routine of Sunday pakoras, which gave comfort.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when the laughing stopped?
qa.a: Mehak might have felt confused or worried, not knowing Devika had suddenly remembered Nani.

grounding: A child's diary shows grieving in bursts, asking repeated questions, and being comforted by honest answers and steady routine.

passage:
In the Himachal village, Omkar's Dadaji had died three days ago. The house was full of relatives and whispers, and nobody cooked the usual rajma.
Omkar kept going to the goat shed. He fed the goats, then sat and cried. Then he chased the kid goat around, laughing.
Later he asked his mother, "Where is Dadaji now?" She hugged him. "Dadaji's body has stopped, and he won't come back. But you can remember him with the goats."
Next morning, Dolma from next door came with a basket, as she always did. "Feed them with me?"
They fed the goats together. Omkar didn't talk much, but he did it every morning after that.

qa.q: Where did Omkar keep going?
qa.a: To the goat shed.

qa.q: What does Omkar crying and then chasing the kid goat show?
qa.a: It shows he felt deep sadness that came in bursts, mixed with moments of normal play.

qa.q: How did his mother and Dolma help Omkar?
qa.a: His mother gave an honest answer and a way to remember Dadaji, and Dolma kept a steady routine of feeding the goats with him.

qa.q: How might Dolma see Omkar's quietness?
qa.a: Dolma likely understood he was grieving and chose to be there without pushing him to talk.

grounding: In a village, a grieving child cries, plays, and asks where his grandfather is, and routine with honest answers helps him.

passage: In their flat in south London, Kofi asked his dad the same question for the fourth time that week. "But where is Grandma Esi now?" Sami sat down beside him again. "Her body stopped working, and she died. She isn't in pain. We keep her with us by remembering her." Kofi nodded, then ran outside to kick his football against the wall with his friends, shouting and laughing. An hour later he came in, went to his room and shut the door. Sami knocked softly and found him holding Grandma Esi's woolly hat. He sat on the bed without speaking. "Is it bad that I was laughing?" Kofi asked. "No. Both are allowed." That evening they still had stew at seven, and Sami still read a chapter at bedtime, like every night.

qa.q: What was Kofi holding when Sami found him?
qa.a: Grandma Esi's woolly hat.

qa.q: Why did Kofi ask whether it was bad that he had been laughing?
qa.a: He felt guilty and confused, worried that playing happily meant he didn't miss Grandma Esi enough.

qa.q: Which choices protected Kofi during his grief?
qa.a: Honest, simple answers each time he asked, sitting with him quietly, and keeping routines like stew at seven and the bedtime chapter.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sami to answer the same question again and again?
qa.a: Sami may be grieving too, yet stays patient and honest each time, which could be tiring but gives Kofi steadiness.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age child grieving a grandparent in bursts, with repeated questions, normal play and sudden withdrawal, supported by honest answers and routine.
